entries.title: It’s already illegal for noncitizens to vote in state elections. However, it will be on West Virginia ballots this November.
entries.summary:
West Virginia voters will consider a ballot measure saying only U.S. citizens can vote in elections. However, that’s already the law.

It’s already illegal for noncitizens to vote in state elections. However, it will be on West Virginia ballots this November. appeared first on Mountain State Spotlight, West Virginia's civic newsroom.
entries.content:
On Election Day, Nov. 3, West Virginia voters will consider a constitutional amendment permitting only United States citizens to vote in state elections — the thing is, that’s already the law.

Here’s why it’s on your ballot and what you should know.

No major effect … at least for now

Though the amendment looks lengthy, only a small part of it is new language.

The constitution, now, says that voters must be citizens of the state.

The amendment would change that to, “Only citizens of the United States who are citizens of this state shall be entitled to vote at all elections held within the counties in which they respectively reside.”

But in practice, the amendment doesn’t change West Virginia elections — noncitizens are already prohibited from voting. 

The citizenship requirement is specified in state law.

In a video Secretary of State Kris Warner and Chief Legal Counsel Dave Cook released about the amendment last week, Cook noted that it doesn’t change voter requirements — people won’t be required to prove their U.S. citizenship by showing birth certificates or similar documents.

But Sen. Patricia Rucker, R-Jefferson and the lead sponsor of Joint Resolution 9, which made way for the amendment proposal, said she wants to see further legislation focused on noncitizen voting that would require such verification.

Rucker, a naturalized citizen from Venezuela, said she introduced it when she realized the language was missing from the constitution and because she believes people should prove they are U.S. citizens while registering to vote.

“I became a citizen after waiting my turn, spending my money and doing it the right way,” she said. 

The House of Delegates and state Senate unanimously passed the proposal. 

If voters approve the amendment, it would be harder to change in the future than the Legislature’s usual process of voting to repeal or pass a law.  The West Virginia constitution is the supreme law of the state. 

The Legislature would have to pass another resolution proposing the repeal of the amendment and put it on the ballot again. Repeal would take a majority vote of citizens.

Is noncitizen voting a problem? 

Judy Ball, co-president of the League of Women Voters of West Virginia, said her organization opposes the amendment because it promotes harmful, divisive myths and reduces trust in the electoral process.

She also noted that if additional proof of identity documents were required in the future, the challenge and expense of securing those documents could make it harder to vote for West Virginians.

“It’s trying to solve a problem that does not exist,” Ball, of Morgantown, said. “You repeat a lie often enough, people start believing it.”

Ball noted that people must already attest during voter registration that they’re citizens, and that it’s a deportable offense for a noncitizen to register or vote.

West Virginia’s constitutional amendment vote isn’t happening in a vacuum.

President Donald Trump has been falsely claiming that noncitizen voting is a rampant problem, and experts have increasingly questioned the basis for those claims. 

In 2025, many state election officials began using the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ (USCIS) Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program to check voter citizenship. They found only 0.04% of voter verification cases were returned as noncitizens.

Still, five other states have introduced ballot measures requiring U.S. citizenship for voting.

Trump has threatened the U.S. Congress by saying he will refuse to sign any legislation until lawmakers pass the SAVE America Act, which would impose much more stringent requirements on all voters nationwide to prove their citizenship. 

As for documents proving citizenship, the Bipartisan Policy Center said these requirements would make voting harder for even eligible citizens like married women and others, who often lack documents like birth certificates and passports.

Full text of West Virginia’s proposed amendment

When you’re in the voting booth, you’ll see the amendment has this title, summary and its full text:

Title of Amendment: “Amendment 1: Citizenship Requirement to Vote in West Virginia Elections Amendment”

Summary of Purpose: “This amendment provides that in all elections held in West Virginia only citizens of the United States who are citizens of this state are qualified to vote.”

Full Text of the Amendment: §4-1. Only citizens of the United States who are citizens of this state shall be entitled to vote at all elections held within the counties in which they respectively reside; but a person who is a minor, or who has been declared mentally incompetent by a court of competent jurisdiction, or who is under conviction of treason, felony or bribery in an election, or who has not been a resident of the state and of the county in which he or she offers to vote, for 30 days next preceding such offer, shall not be permitted to vote while such disability continues; and, a person in the military, naval, or marine service of the United States shall not be deemed a resident of this state by reason of being stationed therein.

It’s already illegal for noncitizens to vote in state elections. However, it will be on West Virginia ballots this November. appeared first on Mountain State Spotlight, West Virginia's civic newsroom.

entries.title: West Virginia groups and local governments demand data center oversight. The state is continuing to develop them anyway.
entries.summary:
West Virginia’s extractive history with developers worries residents as the state signs data center deals with companies

West Virginia groups and local governments demand data center oversight. The state is continuing to develop them anyway. appeared first on Mountain State Spotlight, West Virginia's civic newsroom.
entries.content:
As grassroots groups spring up in opposition to data centers ahead of the midterm elections, city and county governments are looking for ways to exercise their authority and oversight over when, where and if data centers come to their communities. 

The Putnam County Commission signed a resolution in September to hold data center developers accountable to a list of rules. The resolution sets the expectation that data centers will take full cost responsibility for utilities, provide water protection and mitigate the light and noise they produce. 

The commission signed the resolution after Google announced it planned to build a new data center in Buffalo.

Jordan Charbonneau said the Putnam County Commission’s resolution is “a good sign” that more people are concerned about the effects data centers could have on their community.

But, she said, “because of the state law, it makes you have not a lot of faith that these are going to mean anything.”

Charbonneau and her husband Scott Lanham live on an off-the-grid farm in Putnam County, nowhere near the Buffalo data center. Their land is being upended by a gas pipeline to power the Monarch Compute Campus data center development in neighboring Mason County.

They spent three years building their dream off-the-grid home. They live off the land, shower with collected rainwater and get their electricity from solar panels. In August, they found out that a mile-long, 100 feet wide, natural gas pipeline could go through their land and pass within a minute’s walk of their house. 

The couple lives on a parcel of land that Lanham’s father purchased in the 1960s. His sister and brother have their own homes on the land, and his other sister lives nearby. 

Land agents with Brown Resource Group surveyed the land and marked where the pipeline would go. The family has not signed the easement agreement that would give away roughly a mile of their land. 

Charbonneau said that even looking at the survey markers and imagining where the pipeline would be was upsetting. 

“It makes you sad,” she said. “I was crying looking at the blue markers the first day.” 

When state lawmakers took away locals’ say

A resolution, like the one the Putnam County Commission passed, is a statement of a governing body’s opinion. Legislation passed by state lawmakers last year stripped local governments of their authority to do more than offer that.

House Bill 2014, signed into law by Gov. Patrick Morrisey in April 2025, created rules for large-scale data centers in West Virginia and gave the authority and oversight of those rules to the state Department of Commerce. Local governments currently have no power in these decisions.

Amid statewide pushback against the bill, Morrisey announced in August, a plan that made collaboration with local communities a pillar of the process. But the state and technology companies have moved ahead with projects as town and county governments are left in the dark. 

Locals aren’t waiting to be invited into the process.

Putnam United, a grassroots group seeking greater resident involvement in the data center approval and construction process, presented the Putnam County Commission with the resolution, which all three commissioners signed. 

Residents and activists from Mason to Tucker County have formed similar groups across the state.

Jessica Lacy, a member of Putnam United and candidate for Buffalo Town Council, lives three doors down from where Google’s data center construction is to begin next year. She recognizes that state law took the local authority, but believes her county officials should be doing more, like commissioning an independent study into the flooding risks of the data center. 

“For us, this is just a starting point, not a finish line.”

Michael Mosteller is running to represent Putnam in the House of Delegates. He was a member of Putnam United before he left to focus on his campaign. 

He said that until H.B. 2014 is repealed, attempts by city and county governments to oversee large data centers are unenforceable. 

All three commissioners are Republican. Mosteller said he hoped lawmakers in Charleston would see the pushback against the bill by county officials of their own party and follow suit in the statehouse. 

C.D. Caldwell is running against Mosteller but was unavailable for comment. In a candidate interview last week, he said he sees both opportunities and challenges from data centers.

Google did not respond to request for comment.

Local governments look for opportunities for oversight

Mosteller has been trying to convince county commissions and town councils to sue the state on the constitutionality of the bill, with no success.

But for the past year, local governments have tried different ways to exercise oversight and authority where they can. 

The Davis Town Council voted unanimously last May to oppose a nearby planned data center complex.

In February, Morrisey announced the state’s first certified high-impact data center in Berkeley County. 

Almost immediately, the Berkeley County Commission had questions about the impacts on their community. It was five months before Larry Pack, state treasurer, released a tax analysis of the Berkeley County data center.

The commission also asked about stormwater. The Department of Environmental Protection told them that, despite local zoning controls being stripped by state law, the county is responsible for handling stormwater runoff surrounding the data center site. 

Other local governments have tried a different approach. 

In Charleston, the city council is focusing on the smaller data centers not covered by the state’s data center law. 

Council member Emmett Pepper proposed an ordinance earlier this month after hearing talk of smaller-scale data centers coming nearby. The ordinance would require data centers operating in Charleston to get council approval. They must be set back from property lines, prove they won’t use too much water or overload the energy grid, provide an emergency response plan and have a decommission plan ready. 

House Bill 2014 gives the state control over high-impact data centers, but Pepper says small data centers are also cause for concern. His ordinance would create a city law. 

A data center is considered “high-impact” by the state if it demands 90 megawatts of power or more. Pepper said an 89-megawatt data center would be roughly the size of a Target store and would use the same amount of energy as the entire city of Charleston.

The proposed ordinance, co-sponsored by Councilmembers Joe Solomon and Frank Annie, aims to fill a gap that Pepper saw as an opportunity for local control. 

“If we don’t do anything, then they can just come in and operate just like any business can,” he said. 

Up in Wheeling, the city council published a drafted ordinance to include regulations on data centers in industrial districts.

The ordinance comes after Silicon Foundation Energy purchased the former historic Centre Foundry near Wheeling and announced a 10-megawatt data center. 

Sen. Laura Chapman, R-Ohio, and Del. Shawn Fluharty, D-Ohio, are running against each other to represent Wheeling in the Senate. Neither candidate responded to requests for comment, but Fluharty voted against House Bill 2014 and has publicly opposed it. Chapman voted for House Bill 2014 and has spoken highly of it.

Construction goes on

Nscale’s Monarch data center in Mason County was one of the first major data center projects announced in West Virginia in 2023.

It’s been subject to multiple controversies and made national news after flooding nearby residential neighborhoods. Charbonneau and Lanham said they haven’t seen much coverage on the natural gas pipeline that will be coming through their land in Putnam to power it. 

Lanham said it would “ruin” their land if the gas pipeline goes through. 

He said a land agent from Brown Resource Group came to his brother’s door and asked him to sign and allow them to build the pipeline. When his brother asked where the pipeline would be going, the land agent would not answer him. 

Charbonneau found out from online research that the gas will be powering Nscale’s Monarch data center campus in Mason County.

Nscale did not respond to a request for comment for this story. 

When reached by phone, Adam Ellis, President of Operations at Brown Resource Group, declined to comment.

The family hopes their opposition will delay the pipeline until a change in state leadership but don’t feel optimistic.

Lanham is concerned that, in the past, large companies have never faced opposition by the state. 

“They got used to doing almost anything they wanted for years around here, and they’re almost getting away with it now,” he said. 

West Virginia groups and local governments demand data center oversight. The state is continuing to develop them anyway. appeared first on Mountain State Spotlight, West Virginia's civic newsroom.
